AFM Mesbahuddin, Ahsanul Karim with Tanvir Hossain, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Md Jashimuddin with Shah Abdul Hatem, Assistant Attorneys-General—For State-Opposite-Party No. 1 
Shahidul Islam Khan, Advocate—For Opposite-Party No. 2.
parties:
Sabira Sultana ------- Petitioner
Vs
State and another ------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Md Nazrul Islam Talukder J : On an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure filed by the accused-petitioner, a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the impugned proceedings of Special Case No. 13 of 2010 arising out of Dhanmondi Police Station Case No. 21 dated 26-11-2009 under sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, now pending in the Court of Special Judge, Court No. 7, Dhaka should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. During investigation of the case, the Assistant Director Anti-Corruption Commission, Jessore being appointed as investigating officer went to the place of occurrence, recorded the statements of witnesses and seized the necessary papers and documents. 

 4. Having found a prima-facie case, the investigation officer submitted charge-sheet No.139 dated 25-7-2010 against the accusedpetitioner under sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. It may be mentioned here that the accused-petitioner appeared before the Court with an application under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for pre-arrest bail. Upon hearing the parties, this Court by an order dated 8-12-2009 enlarged the accused-petitioner on ad-interim anticipatory bail for a period of 6 (six) months or till submission of the police report whichever is earlier. After expiry of the anticipatory bail, the accused-petitioner voluntarily surrendered before the Court of Special Judge, Court No.7, Dhaka for regular bail and the learned Judge upon hearing the parties enlarged her on regular bail and the aforesaid fact is very much evident from the order No.7 dated 9-1-2011 passed by the Special Judge, Court No.7, Dhaka. 

 8. At the very outset, Mr Ahsanul Karim, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioner, submits that in view of the allegation that the accused-petitioner has concealed the properties worth Taka 30,14,755.84 in the income tax return in the tax assessment year 2008-2009, it may so happen that subsequently, the accused-petitioner has acquired the said property after the closure of the tax assessment year 2008-09, and accordingly, she showed the properties worth Taka 30,14,755.84 in the wealth statement submitted to the Anti-Corruption, and on this score, it cannot be said that the petitioner has committed any offence under sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 and, as such, the petitioner cannot be held liable for the alleged concealment of properties in the income tax return. He next submits that even if the accused-petitioner committed any offence in respect of fiscal claim, the accused-petitioner may be brought within the ambit of offence punishable under sections 165/166 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, and, as such, the allegation allegedly brought against the accused-petitioner cannot be brought within the preview of offence punishable under sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, and in such a posture of things, the accused-petitioner cannot be held liable for the alleged offence brought against her. He then submits that according to the allegation, the accused-petitioner purchased a flat for a consideration of Taka 16,44,300 but during investigation, it was found that actually, she purchased the flat for a consideration of Taka 38,48,000. Mentioning the aforesaid fact, the learned Advocate submits that the consideration money as stated in the registered document has been properly shown in the wealth statement but the certificate or receipt allegedly procured from a developer company cannot prevail over the registered instrument in view of section 58(c) of the Registration Act, and in such a position, it cannot be said that the accused-petitioner has committed any offence under sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. He lastly submits that the shop allegedly mentioned in the FIR was not purchased by the accused-petitioner, rather she only entered into an agreement for purchasing the same, and in view of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and section 49 of the Registration Act, no" immovable property can be acquired without registration of document, and, as such, accused-petitioner was not under the obligation to show the said property (shop) in her wealth statement or in the income tax return. He lastly submits that the allegations which have been brought against the accused-petitioner are totally unfounded, baseless and concocted, and, as such, the initiation and continuation of the impugned proceedings amount to sheer abuse of process of the Court, and under the given context, the accused-petitioner has prayed for quashing the impugned proceedings, and considering the aforesaid aspects of the case, the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioner should not be continued and the same should be quashed. 

 9. On the other hand, Mr Md Shahidul Islam Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the informant-opposite-party No.2, the Anti-Corruption Commission, submits that there is no valid ground for quashing the impugned proceedings and that the allegations leveled against the petitioner in the FIR and in the charge-sheet attract the elements of offence under sections 26(2) and 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. He next submits that the grounds taken in the application are based on defence materials and defence pleas which cannot be gone into in the present forum for quashing the impugned proceedings. Learned Advocate for opposite-Party No.2, in support of his submission, relied on the decisions taken in the cases of Rahela Khatun vs Abul Hasan, 48 DLR (AD) 213 and Hossain Mohammad Ershad vs State, 43 DLR (AD) 50. He then submits that none of the grounds taken in the application falls within the principle as set out in the decision taken in the case of All Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16. He lastly submits that there are specific allegations against the accused-petitioner and that the aforesaid allegations were prima-facie found true by the investigating officer and the learned trial Judge accordingly framed charge against the accused-petitioner under the aforesaid relevant laws, and considering all the aspects of the case, the impugned proceeding cannot be quashed. 

 10. We have also gone through the application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the materials annexed thereto. We have also considered the grounds taken in the miscellaneous case and the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. In view of the submissions and counter-submissions advanced by the learned Advocates for the respective parties, a pertinent question arises whether the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioner should be quashed. To decide this issue, it is necessary to see the extent of the principles and categories of cases in which High Court Division may invoke its extra-ordinary power and authority under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings. 

 11. In the case of All Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16, it has been spelt out that in order to bring a case within the purview of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the purpose of quashing a Criminal proceeding, one of the following conditions must be fulfilled: 

 (1)	Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused. 

 (4) In a case where the allegations in the FIR or the petition of complaint, even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence as alleged. 

 (5) The allegations against the accused although constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge". 

 18. It is now well-settled that whether the allegations leveled against the accused-petitioner are true or false can only be thrashed out or gone into during trial of the case. 

 It is settled principle of law that a disputed question of fact cannot be decided by this Court and that a Criminal proceedings cannot be quashed on the basis of defence materials or on the basis of defence plea. The aforesaid view finds support in the case of Rahela Khatun vs Abul Hossain reported in 48 DLR (AD) (1996) 213 wherein it has been held: 

 "A Criminal proceeding cannot be quashed on the basis of defence materials which are still not part of the materials for the prosecution. The High Court Division deviated from a well-known norm of disposal of an application for quashing criminal proceeding by taking into account the defence version of the case." 

 19. Similar view has been expressed in the case of Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs The State reported in 43 DLR (AD) 50 wherein it has been decided: 

 20. The aforesaid view finds support in the decision in the case of Faruk Ahamed vs Abdul Kader Chowdhury, 30 DLR (AD) (1986) 18, Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs State, 14 BLD (AD) (1994) 1.61 and Amal Cabraal vs Golam Murtaza reported in 55 DLR 492. Moreover it is also settled principle of law that under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, this Court is not in a position to draw inquiry as to truth or otherwise of the asserted facts. 

 21. In the case of Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs State reported in 45 DLR (AD) 48 wherein it has been laid down: 

 "In a proceeding under this provision, the Court should not be drawn in an enquiry as to the truth or otherwise of the facts which are not in the prosecution case." 

 22. In view of the circumstances of the case, the allegations made in the FIR and charge-sheet and the settled propositions of law, we are not in a position to dispose of the disputed questions of fact which may be traced out or decided during trial of the case and the disputed questions may be resolved only on evidence to be adduced by the concerned parties. 

 24. We have gone through the decisions referred to by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No.2. We find that the sum and sub-stance of those cases is that the impugned proceedings cannot be quashed unless the allegation falls within the categories and principles for quashing the impugned proceedings. Under the circumstances, the decisions referred to by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No.2 appear to be applicable to the instant proceedings. 

 25. We have also gone through the relevant laws which have been mentioned by the learned Advocates for the petitioner during their submissions. Within the four corners of those laws, we do not find that the prosecution case initiated against accused-petitioner is barred by any law, and, as such, there is no legal bar to proceed with the case against the accused-petitioner. 

 26. From the foregoing discussions and regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case, and the propositions of law discussed above, we are led to hold that the impugned proceeding initiated against the accused-petitioner cannot be quashed and the same is maintainable and sustainable in the eye of law. 

 27. Having considered all the aspects of the case, we do not find any merit in this Rule. 

 The learned Special Judge is directed to proceed with the trial of the case in accordance with law.
